Irreconcilable
ĭr-rĕk´ŏn-sī-la-bl
adj. (not to be brought to agreement or friendship; implacable)
Latin in-, not, and reconciliare, to bring back into council or fellowship. The AV's word for the disposition is implacable and trucebreakers.

Biblical Definition

The irreconcilable man will not be brought to terms. Paul lists the disposition among the marks of a reprobate mind: “without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” (Rom 1:31), and among the perils of the last days: “trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent” (2Ti 3:3). Against it stands the Christian's obligation: “first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift” (Mat 5:24) — the worshipper leaves the altar to do it. The rule is stated with its limits acknowledged: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18). And the ground of all of it is the cross, “that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby” (Eph 2:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines irreconcilable as not to be reconciled; that cannot be appeased or brought to friendly terms; implacable; and, of things, incapable of being made to agree or be consistent.

expand to see more

IRRECONCILABLE, a. Not to be reconciled; that cannot be appeased or brought to friendly accord; implacable; as an irreconcilable enemy or quarrel.

2. Not to be made consistent or congruous; as irreconcilable stories or statements.

IRRECONCILABLY, adv. In a manner that precludes reconciliation.

Key Scripture

Rom 1:31 — "Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful:"

2Ti 3:3 — "Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,"

Mat 5:24 — "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."

Rom 12:18 — "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

Eph 2:16 — "And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:"

Modern Corruption

Romans 12:18 is read as an escape clause, and it is a boundary on the other man's conduct rather than on one's own effort.

expand to see more

Romans 12:18 has two qualifications and they are almost always misapplied. If it be possible concedes that some reconciliations fail, because the other party may refuse and no one can be compelled into peace. As much as lieth in you is the demanding half: whatever portion of the matter is yours, all of it must be spent. The verse is not a permission to give up early. It is a statement that a Christian's responsibility ends at the boundary of his own conduct — and that within that boundary there is no residue left unspent.

Matthew 5:23–24 shows how far the obligation runs, and the direction of the offence is the surprising part. It is not if thou hast ought against thy brother but if thy brother hath ought against thee. The man with the grievance is elsewhere; the man at the altar is the one told to go. He leaves his gift, travels, and is reconciled first, and only then comes back to worship. A church full of unaddressed grievances is not offering acceptable worship, and the Lord puts the burden on whoever is aware of the problem rather than on whoever is at fault.

Ephesians 2:16 supplies the pattern and the power, and its verb is violent: reconciled both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby. The enmity was not negotiated away; it was killed, and killed at cost. That is why a Christian's refusal to be reconciled with a brother is so serious a thing — it denies in practice what he claims to have received, and the parable of the unforgiving servant applies the arithmetic. Romans 1:31 puts implacable in a list of what human nature comes to when God gives it over, which means that implacability is not a personality but a symptom.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aspondos (G786), implacable, admitting no truce; diallassomai (G1259), to be reconciled; katallasso (G2644), to reconcile; apokatallasso (G604), to reconcile fully.

expand to see more

Greek aspondos (G786) — implacable, refusing a truce; Romans 1:31, 2 Timothy 3:3 — both occurrences.

Greek diallagethi (G1259) — be reconciled; Matthew 5:24 only.

Greek apokatallasso (G604) — to reconcile completely; Ephesians 2:16, Colossians 1:20–22.

Usage

"“As much as lieth in you” — the demanding half of the verse."

"“Thy brother hath ought against thee” — and thou leavest the gift."

"“Having slain the enmity thereby” — it was killed, not negotiated."
